title: My own work
hook: better one's own duty done imperfectly than another's done well (Bhagavad Gita 3.35)

segments.voice: Yesterday, vocation: Luther's cobbler, called to his bench. Your line was my calling. Which ordinary station did you treat as a calling? Today the Work block turns to Hindu, Sikh, Muslim and Buddhist voices. Day eight hundred ninety-two.

Scrolling at midnight, and everyone else's work looks better. The friend who started a bakery. The cousin who travels for her job. The stranger whose desk is a beach. Some nights a person can spend more energy wishing for someone else's path than walking their own. The Bhagavad Gita has a line for that. This block has already met Arjuna between two armies, ready to drop his bow. By the third chapter, his charioteer Krishna is still answering him, and the answer turns from the battlefield to a question of whose work is whose. Today's word.
screen: `EVERYONE ELSE'S WORK LOOKS BETTER.` → `WHOSE WORK IS WHOSE?` → `KRISHNA ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself, in the third chapter of the Gita. In paraphrase: better your own duty, even done imperfectly, than another's duty done well. The Sanskrit word is svadharma, your own dharma, your own duty or path. Second, the surprise. The verse doesn't say do your own work well. It says your own work done badly is better than someone else's done brilliantly. That can sound backward. Krishna isn't praising sloppiness. He's saying something about where a person belongs. Borrowed work, even when it looks good, isn't yours. The verse goes further, saying that another's duty is full of danger. Third, Hindus read this in more than one way. Some older commentators tied your own duty to your place in society, the duties of your family and station. Some modern readers hear it more as your own nature: the gifts, temperament and responsibilities that are actually yours, not the ones you envy. Both readings are found among Hindus today, and teachers can disagree sharply about the first. Fourth, the ordinary version. A parent trying to raise their children the way another family does. A coworker doing someone else's job because it's more visible. An artist copying a style that isn't theirs. The Gita's question is quiet and hard: what's actually mine to do? By the end of the Gita, Arjuna says he will do as Krishna asks. On an ordinary day the duty in front of us is usually smaller. An email, a dish, a conversation we've been avoiding. Imperfect, and our own.
screen: `BETTER YOUR OWN, IMPERFECT.` · `NOT ANOTHER'S, DONE WELL.` · `STATION, OR YOUR OWN NATURE?` · `WHAT'S ACTUALLY MINE TO DO?` · then, large: `SVADHARMA.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone whose work or life you've been quietly wishing were yours. Let the picture come, and don't scold yourself for it. Then gently set it down, like putting someone else's coat back on the hook. Now ask: what's in front of me that only I can do? A person who needs me in particular, a task that's mine. Let it come into focus. It may look small or unfinished. Breathe with it. If you pray, you can offer that work in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
My own work. From the Bhagavad Gita: better your own duty, done imperfectly, than another's done well. Today's word.
Your line: my own work. Today, do your own work, not someone else's. When you catch yourself comparing, come back to the task in front of you. Day eight hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Hindus read and recite the Bhagavad Gita at home and in temples and study groups; Gita 3.35 is often taught as a call to do one's own duty faithfully rather than imitate another's.
